1: As agent applications grow more complex, developers have to deal with tool calling, knowledge access, state management and multi-agent collaboration. Building all of that from scratch is not only a lot of work; connecting the modules and controlling how they run is complex too.
2: Agent frameworks wrap up these common capabilities and offer a unified way to build agents. Below are several representative agent development frameworks.
4: LangChain was released in 2022 and is one of the earlier open-source frameworks for building large-model applications. Early on it mainly organised components such as models, prompts and external data, then gradually extended to tool calling and agents. Today LangChain treats the agent as an important part of the framework and provides components such as models, tools and middleware, so you can build agents with tool-calling ability quickly.
5: LangChain's core way of running is to put the large model and the tools into a loop. The model receives the user's task and the tools it may use and judges from the current information whether to generate a result directly or call a tool. If it calls a tool, the framework runs that tool and gives the result back to the model. The model keeps judging with the new information until it no longer needs a tool and produces the final result. The official documentation calls this the Agent Loop, as shown below.
6: For example, a travel assistant can be given tools for weather, maps and web search. When the user asks “plan me a one-day trip to Hangzhou tomorrow”, the model can judge that it needs weather and attraction information, call the corresponding tools and use those results to finish the itinerary.
7: A Tool is an important way to implement external capability: essentially a callable function with clear input and output, used to fetch real-time data, run code, query a database or operate an external system. Once the developer gives the agent the tools it needs, the model can decide from the current task when to call which tool and what parameters to pass.
8: This component-based approach is a key feature of LangChain. It provides fairly unified interfaces for different models and tools, so developers can combine components in one framework without handling the calling logic between each model and each external capability separately. It therefore suits building tool-calling agents quickly and helps beginners understand how an agent runs.
10: LlamaIndex was released in 2022, initially to solve the problem of connecting large models with external data. It offers data loading, indexing, retrieval and querying, so enterprise documents, databases and other external data can be brought into a large-model application. On that basis LlamaIndex gradually added agents and workflows, letting an agent use that data for more complex tasks.
11: A large model does not know a company's internal product documents, business material and databases. When an agent needs that data for a task, it first has to find information relevant to the current task. LlamaIndex can load, organise and index external data and then retrieve and query it through components such as Retriever and Query Engine. A Query Engine can take a natural-language question, look up relevant data in the index and also be wrapped as a tool an agent can call. As shown below, after receiving a user task the agent can choose the appropriate query tool to get information and then let the model analyse it and produce the final result. In this way the whole external dataset does not have to be put into the context; relevant data is queried and used as the task requires.
12: For example, a business-analysis agent can be given tools for product-document lookup and business-data lookup. When the user asks to compare the feature differences of two products, the agent calls the product-material tool; if the user then asks about their sales, it calls the business-data tool. For a more complex question the agent can call several data tools in succession and combine the results from different sources.
13: LlamaIndex was not originally designed specifically for agent development; its strength is data and knowledge handling. It lets a large model retrieve documents and organises different data and query capabilities into tools an agent can choose and use. It suits knowledge-base Q&A, document analysis, multi-source querying and agent applications that need access to large numbers of enterprise documents, knowledge bases or structured data.
15: AutoGen was released by Microsoft Research in 2023 and is a representative open-source framework in multi-agent development. Its core idea is Multi-Agent Conversation: several agents complete a task by talking to one another.
16: AutoGen designs agents as conversational, customisable entities; an agent can be made of a large model, tools, human input or a combination of these. Developers can also define how agents interact, giving different agents different conversation patterns. The overall design is shown below.
17: The figure reflects two important design ideas in AutoGen. First, different agents can have different abilities. Second, several agents can be organised through different conversation patterns to communicate and collaborate in different ways.
18: For example, in a software-development task you can set up one agent to analyse the requirement, one to write code and another to check the result. After the coding agent generates code it sends the result to the checking agent; if a problem is found, the checking agent can feed it back to the coding agent to keep revising until the task requirements are met.
19: AutoGen currently offers two levels of capability: AgentChat and Core. AgentChat is the high-level interface for building single-agent and multi-agent applications, providing components such as Agent and Team. Developers can put several agents into a Team and organise collaboration by taking turns or dynamically choosing the next agent. Core is event-driven and provides the low-level capability for more flexible and extensible multi-agent systems.
20: AutoGen's distinguishing feature is that it makes communication and collaboration between agents the focus of the framework design, so it suits complex tasks that need several agents sharing the work. A multi-agent system needs extra design of each agent's responsibilities and how they collaborate; for simple tasks there is usually no need for several agents.
22: CrewAI also targets multi-agent collaboration but organises it more like a real team. Developers can define roles, goals and tools for each agent and then organise them through tasks and processes. CrewAI mainly offers two ways to organise: Crews, which emphasises autonomous collaboration among agents, and Flows, which emphasises structured process control.
23: CrewAI's official framework structure is shown below.
24: In a Crew, an Agent can be understood as a team member with specific responsibilities, a Task is the concrete work to be done, a Process sets how agents and tasks are executed, and the Crew organises the agents and tasks to reach the final goal together.
25: For example, to produce an industry research report you can create a research agent, a writing agent and a review agent. The research agent finds and organises material, the writing agent forms the report from the findings and the review agent checks it for problems. Different agents take different responsibilities and complete the work together through the links between tasks.
26: A Flow can organise task execution along a predefined process and supports conditionals, loops and state management. Crew and Flow can be combined: for example, use a Flow to control the overall business process and call a Crew inside one complex step, where several agents collaborate on the task.
27: CrewAI's distinguishing feature is organising multi-agent collaboration through roles, tasks and teams, in a way that resembles how a real team divides work. It suits multi-agent applications with clear role and task boundaries, such as research, content generation, data analysis and review.
29: LangGraph was released by the LangChain team in 2024 as a low-level orchestration framework for building and managing long-running, stateful agents. Instead of using pre-built agents directly, LangGraph lets developers define the agent's execution structure explicitly, which suits agents whose flow involves state, branching, loops and human involvement.
30: LangGraph can build both Workflows with a relatively clear execution path and Agents whose next step is decided dynamically by the large model. A Workflow can predefine the task's execution path and organise steps through sequencing, parallelism, routing and loops; an Agent can decide the next operation dynamically from the current state and tool results. In practice the two can be combined: the Workflow sets the overall process and the Agent handles the steps that need dynamic decisions.
31: The Workflow and Agent patterns LangGraph supports are shown below.
32: To implement these different ways of executing, LangGraph describes the task's execution with a graph whose three basic concepts are State, Node and Edge. State holds the information to be shared during execution; a Node is a concrete processing step, such as calling the large model, retrieving knowledge or running a tool; an Edge connects nodes and decides which node the task goes to next.
33: For example, a knowledge Q&A agent can first analyse the user's question, then retrieve knowledge, generate an answer and check the result. If the check fails, a conditional branch can send the task back to the retrieval node; if it passes, the task goes to the final output node. Throughout, the user's question, retrieval results and intermediate answers can all live in the State and be shared between nodes.
34: This design differs from relying entirely on the large model to decide the next step. LangGraph lets you lay out the task's general execution structure in advance and use the model for decisions at the nodes that need them. That keeps the agent's ability to judge from the actual situation while allowing control over the critical execution paths.
35: Besides the graph structure and state management, LangGraph offers Durable Execution and Human-in-the-loop capabilities. A long-running task can save its execution state and continue after an interruption; before an important operation the agent can be paused to wait for human review or a state change. The official documentation therefore positions LangGraph as a low-level orchestration framework for long-running, stateful agents.
36: LangGraph gives finer-grained control over state and execution paths, but it also requires more flow design from the developer. For a simple tool-calling agent there is no need to build a complex graph from the start. The official documentation also suggests starting from LangChain's agent if you are just learning about agents or need a higher-level abstraction.
38: MS-Agent is the lightweight open-source agent development framework from the ModelScope community. Aimed mainly at tasks that need autonomous exploration and multi-step execution, it offers model calling, tool access and multi-agent collaboration for building applications such as deep research, document analysis and code generation.
39: MS-Agent's basic component is LLMAgent, which organises large-model conversation and tool calling. Developers can specify the model, prompt and tools through a configuration file. After receiving a user task, LLMAgent gives the task and the available tools to the model, which decides the next operation. If a tool is needed, the framework runs it and hands the result back to the model to continue, until the model's reply no longer includes a tool call or the configured maximum number of rounds is reached.
40: The basic run flow of LLMAgent is shown below. After initialising the configuration and preparing messages, the agent loops between model calls and tool execution and compresses the context when needed. The cb in the figure stands for callback, where developers can add logging or other custom handling.
41: Tool access is an important capability of MS-Agent. The framework provides built-in tools for file reading and writing, code execution and task splitting, and also supports connecting external tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). Developers can reuse existing MCP services or write custom tools so the agent can reach the data and external systems the task needs.
42: For tasks that need several steps working together, MS-Agent supports composing different agents into a workflow. LLMAgent handles the steps that need the model to judge and generate, while CodeAgent handles determinate operations executed as code. Developers can organise material analysis, data processing and result generation into one workflow and specify the steps' execution relationships in a configuration file.
43: For example, Code Genesis in the MS-Agent project provides an example of multi-agent collaboration for code generation, dividing the process into design and coding, then checking and optimisation. An architecture agent does the design and a task-splitting tool assigns the work to several coding agents; in the optimisation stage, follow-up changes are split according to build or human-review feedback and handled by the coding agents.
45: Besides agent development frameworks, some model vendors also offer agent development through an SDK (Software Development Kit), wrapping model calling, tool calling and task execution into interfaces, classes and components that help developers create and run agents in their own applications. Agent frameworks and agent SDKs can both build agents; their capabilities overlap somewhat and they differ in organisation and focus. Below are two representative agent SDKs.
47: OpenAI released the OpenAI Agents SDK in 2025, emphasising building agent applications with few core abstractions. With the Agent as the basic execution unit, it provides tool calling, task handoff, run constraints and execution tracing around the agent. Tools query data, run code, call APIs or operate other external systems; Handoffs let the current agent pass a task to another agent better suited to it; Guardrails check the agent's input, output and some tool calls; Tracing records the model generations, tool calls, handoffs and guardrail events that happen during a run.
48: The OpenAI Agents SDK also provides Agent Visualization, which can generate a graph of an agent together with the other agents, Tools and MCP Servers it connects to. Directed connections between agents can represent a handoff, while connections between tools and agents represent tool calls.
49: In a customer-service system, for example, you can set up an entry agent that identifies the user's problem, then an order agent, a refund agent and an FAQ agent for different kinds of business. When the user asks about a refund, the entry agent can hand the task to the refund agent via Handoff; the refund agent then calls tools such as order lookup and refund application as needed. Handoff particularly suits scenarios where different specialist agents handle different tasks.
50: Guardrails and Tracing address the constraints and observability of a running agent. Guardrails can check the agent's input, final output and before/after execution of custom function tools; Tracing records the model generations, tool calls, handoffs and guardrail events of one agent run, helping developers see which steps the agent went through and where a problem appeared.
51: The OpenAI Agents SDK's distinguishing feature is that its core concepts are relatively concentrated. Developers can start with a single agent and Tools and gradually add multi-agent collaboration, Guardrails and Tracing. Compared with LangGraph the design focus differs: LangGraph emphasises fine-grained control of state and workflow, while the OpenAI Agents SDK offers common capabilities around an agent such as tool calling, task handoff, run constraints and execution tracing.
53: The Claude Agent SDK is Anthropic's agent development SDK, originally named Claude Code SDK and later renamed Claude Agent SDK. It opens up the agent capabilities of Claude Code to developers, so they can build agents in their own applications that use tools, access the runtime environment and keep working on tasks.
54: Compared with the agent development tools above, one striking feature of the Claude Agent SDK is that it pays more attention to the agent's access to and operation of the actual runtime environment. Besides calling external tools it provides built-in capabilities for reading files, modifying files and executing commands, so the agent can handle files, run programs and execute commands directly, and can connect more external tools and data through MCP. It also provides permission control, Hooks and Subagents: permission control limits what the agent may do; Hooks add custom handling at key stages such as tool calls; Subagents let part of the work go to an independent sub-agent.
55: While running, the agent judges the next operation from the current task and context, for example reading a file, modifying code or executing a command. Tool results come back to the agent, which keeps judging with the new information until the task is done. The Claude Agent SDK organises this execution and handles tool calling, permission checks and context passing along the way.
56: In a software-development task, for example, the agent can read the project code, modify files as the user requires and then run the tests. If the tests fail, the agent can read the error output and keep revising until the task is complete. In this process the large model understands the task and decides the next operation, while the Claude Agent SDK provides the file system, terminal and tools and manages permissions and the execution process.
57: The Claude Agent SDK suits agent applications that need to access files and a runtime environment, call tools in succession and execute multi-step tasks, especially software development and automation.
58: In real agent development, the runtime environment, context management, permission control, task state and execution feedback are getting more attention. How to organise these capabilities around a large model and manage and control the task's execution has become an important question in agent system design, and that is exactly what Harness addresses.
61: As large-model ability keeps improving, the agent's problem shifts from “can the model complete a task” to “can the model complete real tasks reliably and continuously”. In a simple Q&A the model only has to generate a result from the input; but in complex tasks such as software development, data analysis or business automation, an agent may work for a long time, save progress between steps, call different tools and keep adjusting its next actions from the actual results. Relying only on the model's own reasoning does not guarantee that the task is finally completed correctly.
62: For example, a coding agent may understand the requirement to “change some feature” correctly and generate high-quality code, yet still hit various problems in practice: starting to modify code without reading the project conventions, changing too many files at once, missing necessary steps, losing earlier task progress during execution, or declaring the task done before the code passes its tests. These problems do not come purely from the model's ability but from the working environment it sits in and the way the task is executed.
63: A Harness is a working environment and runtime mechanism built around the large model, defining what information the model can obtain, which operations it can perform, how task state is saved, how completion is judged and how to carry on when something goes wrong. Through these mechanisms the model's individual inferences and actions are organised into a constrained, continuously running task execution whose result can be verified.
64: The point of a Harness is not to further increase the model's knowledge or reasoning but to let the abilities it already has act on real tasks more reliably. The model still understands the task, analyses the problem and decides the next operation; the Harness creates the working conditions the model needs to complete the task and applies constraints and feedback across the execution.
65: Seen as a run, a Harness makes the agent a continuous loop: the agent judges from the current task and state, performs the corresponding operation and takes new results from the environment; those results, once recorded, checked and fed back, become the basis for the next decision. If a result does not meet the requirement, the agent keeps revising and executing; the task only truly ends when the pre-defined completion conditions are met.
66: A Harness differs clearly from a simple prompt or tool call. A prompt mainly tells the model the task goal and behaviour requirements, and tools let the model perform concrete operations, whereas a Harness further concerns how those instructions and tools are organised and managed across the whole execution. It has to let the agent know where to start, how far it has got, which operations it may perform, how results are verified, when it may finish, and how to continue after an interruption. For agents that run long and execute many steps, these mechanisms directly affect whether the task is completed reliably.
68: There is no single way to implement a Harness; different agent systems offer different runtime mechanisms for different tasks. Judging by the problems an agent actually has to solve while running, a Harness can be summed up as five cooperating parts: instructions and context, tools, runtime environment, state and task continuity, and verification and feedback.
70: Instructions and context decide what the agent “knows” in the current task and what it “should follow”.
71: Instructions include not only the task the user just typed but also the system prompt, project rules, coding conventions, business constraints, task boundaries and completion conditions. A coding agent, for example, can learn the directory structure, development conventions, test methods and off-limits areas from AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or project documentation.
72: Context means the effective information given to the model during execution: the user's requirement, previous operations, file contents, tool results and the current task state. Because the model's context window is limited, a Harness usually also has to select, compress and reorganise the context so the model gets what the current task really needs rather than simply appending all history.
73: For complex tasks you can use layered instructions and progressive context loading. First let the agent read the project overview, then load a module's local rules once it enters that module; when a task runs long and the context keeps growing, compress the early process and keep only the key conclusions, task state and information still needed later. These mechanisms keep giving the agent effective information inside a limited context window and constrain its task scope and behaviour through instructions.
75: The large model mainly understands, reasons and produces decisions; reading external information or performing concrete operations still takes tools. Tools therefore decide what actions the agent can actually perform.
76: For a coding agent the common tools include file reading, file modification, code search, shell command execution, Git operations and test tools; for an enterprise agent they may include database queries, knowledge-base retrieval, a browser, business APIs and external systems connected through MCP.
77: At this layer a Harness does more than keep a list of tools: it handles tool descriptions, parameter organisation, call routing, returning execution results and exception handling. After the model decides to “run the project tests”, for example, the Harness has to call the right tool, execute the test command in the specified environment and organise the standard output, error messages and exit status back to the model so the agent can decide the next operation from the result.
78: Tool calling needs corresponding security and permission control. Some tools may only read files, others allow modification; where deleting files, accessing the network, executing system commands or operating production systems is involved, you can restrict by risk level and require human confirmation when necessary. Mechanisms such as Hooks can also be inserted before and after a tool call to check parameters, log execution or block operations that break the rules.
79: In systems that support Subagents, the main agent can hand part of the work to a dedicated subagent. Code search, test analysis or material organisation can be assigned to different subagents and their results summarised. That extends a single agent's task capacity and reduces the pressure of keeping a complex task in one execution context.
81: Tools answer “what can the agent do”; the runtime environment determines “where those operations happen”.
82: For a coding agent the runtime environment may be a local project directory, a container, a virtual machine, a cloud Sandbox or a separate Git Worktree. Reading and modifying files, executing shell commands, installing dependencies and running tests all depend on that environment.
83: The Harness has to prepare and manage the environment: initialise the repository, install dependencies, set environment variables, start necessary services and check whether the environment meets the conditions for the task. For long-running tasks it also has to avoid missing dependencies, failing services or inconsistent resource state during execution.
84: Environment isolation is also an important part of environment management. If several agents or tasks work on the same project at once, operating the same working directory can cause file overwrites and state conflicts. Creating separate Sandboxes, containers or Worktrees for different tasks lets them run in relatively isolated spaces. Even if one task fails, the impact on other tasks and the host environment is reduced.
85: The runtime environment also controls resource access boundaries: restricting the agent to certain directories, only permitting specific network access, blocking sensitive system files, or giving different tasks different access credentials. Tools define which capabilities the agent can use, and the runtime environment limits which files, processes, network and system resources those capabilities can actually affect.
87: A single large-model call has no natural long-term task state, while a complex agent task may last tens of minutes, hours or span several sessions. If task information exists only in the current context, then once that context is compressed, the process is interrupted or the session restarts, the agent may be unable to tell exactly what it has already done.
88: The Harness has to maintain task state: the current goal, how the task was split, the steps already done, the step in progress, files changed, important tool results and what remains to be done.
89: That state can be kept in memory or written to task files, a database, Git history or other external storage. For long-running agents persistent state matters especially. A new agent session can read the progress and key results saved before and continue from the last interruption instead of re-analysing the whole task.
90: State management runs through the task's whole lifecycle. The initial state is created when the task starts, progress and key results are recorded throughout, and the final state is saved on completion; if the task is interrupted by an error, a timeout or a system restart, checkpointing and similar mechanisms can restore it to the previous execution position. For complex tasks involving subagents, each subtask's completion, results and dependencies can be recorded.
91: The point of state and task continuity is to maintain a task execution that can be updated continuously, persisted and restored, so the agent still knows how far the task has got when it runs long or spans sessions.
93: An agent performing an action does not mean the task is correctly done. It may have modified a code file successfully yet the code does not compile; it may have produced an analysis report that misses key data; a business API call may succeed but yield a result that breaks business rules. So a Harness also needs verification and feedback: check the results and give the checks back to the agent.
94: The way to verify depends on the task. For software development you can use unit tests, linting, type checking, compilation and end-to-end tests; for business tasks, business-rule checks, result comparison or an independent evaluator. The core of verification is to provide checkable grounds for completion rather than relying only on the model's own judgement that “the task is done”.
95: Feedback then returns the verification result to the agent. After a failed test, for example, the Harness can give the error messages and relevant logs back to the model, and the agent uses them to analyse the cause, revise the code and test again: “execute → verify → get feedback → fix → verify again”. That loop lets the agent keep correcting earlier decisions from real results instead of finishing right after one operation.
96: A Harness can also add execution control. For example, only allow code to be committed after all tests pass; stop the task or hand it to a human after several consecutive failures; for high-risk operations such as production changes or data deletion, pause the task before execution and require human approval, continuing with confirmation or stopping and adjusting without it.
97: These five parts together support the agent's continuous running: instructions and context provide the goal, rules and necessary information; tools provide the ability to act; the runtime environment hosts those operations and limits resource boundaries; state and task continuity record progress and support recovery; verification and feedback check results and push the agent to keep fixing or finish. Through them the Harness organises the agent's individual model calls into a complete task execution that can run continuously, is constrained and whose results can be verified.
99: An agent and a Harness are not two concepts that replace each other; they sit at different levels. While an agent runs, the large model mainly understands the task, analyses the current information and decides the next operation; the Harness provides instructions and context, tools, the runtime environment, state management and verification feedback around the agent, so its decisions can actually be executed and are constrained and checked along the way.
100: The relationship is one of “decision and execution support”. The agent judges from the current task and available information what to do next, and the Harness provides the tools and environment needed for that operation and records the state and results it produces. Once done, the Harness can verify the result through tests or rule checks and give the feedback to the agent. The agent then judges the next operation from the new state and feedback, and the cycle repeats until the completion conditions are met.
101: For example, a coding agent decides it needs to modify login.py and run the tests. Analysing the code and deciding how to modify it mainly depends on the model's understanding and reasoning; whether login.py may be modified, where to read the file, which tool modifies it, in which Sandbox the test command runs, how progress is saved, how the test result is checked and how to continue after a failure all need the Harness's runtime mechanisms. After a failed test the error output goes back to the agent, which analyses the cause and decides the next change.
102: How complete a Harness is affects the kinds of task an agent can handle. A simple Harness may offer only a few tools and a basic calling mechanism, good for tasks with few steps; a fuller Harness can add context management, environment isolation, task-state persistence, permission control, automatic verification, failure recovery and human approval, letting the agent run longer and more complex tasks. Even with the same large model, different Harnesses give different running conditions, and the agent's ability and stability on complex tasks can differ markedly.
103: Harness and agent frameworks overlap somewhat: both involve tool calling, context management, state management and execution control, but their focus differs. Agent frameworks lean towards the development capabilities for building agents and organising tasks, such as agent definition, tool calling, state management, workflow orchestration and multi-agent collaboration; a Harness focuses more on the support and control built around an agent's running: how to organise the context, how to provide tools and a runtime environment, how to keep the task continuous and how to verify results. As agent frameworks and SDKs keep evolving, some Harness capabilities are also being integrated into them, so there is no absolute functional boundary in implementation.
104: Overall, the relationship between the three can be summarised as: the large model provides the intelligence, the agent organises the decisions, and the Harness guarantees the execution.
105: As the complexity of the tasks an agent executes grows, the role of the Harness becomes more prominent.
107: Below we take DeepSeek Harness as an example to understand further how a Harness is organised in a real agent system.
108: DeepSeek Harness is the open-source agent Harness DeepSeek released in 2026. It organises the tools, Skills, sessions, sandboxes and task execution a model needs to run through a plugin architecture, giving the agent extensible runtime support.
109: DeepSeek understands a runnable agent as:
111: Here the Model understands the task and makes decisions, and the Harness organises the tools, context and execution environment the model needs to complete the task.
112: DeepSeek Harness's core design is “Everything is a Plugin”. Models, tools, Skills, sessions, sandboxes, storage, the execution loop, task scheduling and subagents can all be provided as plugins and organised by the underlying Cordis plugin system. Cordis handles plugin loading and unloading, dependency management and lifecycle management, while different plugins provide the concrete agent capabilities. Developers can combine, replace or extend plugins as needed.

114: For example, using DeepSeek Harness to build a data-analysis agent. The agent reads the data files the user provides, calls the right tools for data processing and analysis and can use Skills for specific analysis tasks. If the task is complex, part of the work can go to a Subagent. The model decides what operation is needed next and the Harness provides and organises the capabilities required for those operations.
115: Besides the plugin design, DeepSeek Harness provides sessions and run records. The system prompt the model sees, tool calls and their results, Subagent scheduling and context injection can be recorded in a session log and viewed through Trajectory. Based on those records a task can be restored, forked, searched and replayed, making it easier for developers to observe and debug the agent's execution.
116: DeepSeek Harness is still in Developer Preview and its core plugins and APIs are still being iterated. It is therefore better treated as a representative case for understanding Harness plugin design and engineering than as an already fixed development standard.
